label: Africa
subtitle: North, West, Central, East & Southern
about: Cuisines of North, West, Central, East and Southern Africa.

label: Moroccan
subtitle: Tagines, couscous, chermoula, preserved lemon
about: This node should represent Morocco specifically, on the Atlantic and Mediterranean edges of northwest Africa between the Rif, Atlas Mountains and Sahara, rather than a generic North African blend. Amazigh, Arab, Andalusi, Jewish, sub-Saharan African and Mediterranean histories all shaped a cuisine built around balanced spices, slow-cooked tagines, steamed couscous, preserved foods and herb-rich marinades. Representative dishes include couscous with vegetables, chicken tagine with preserved lemon and olives, harira and pastilla.
signature_ingredients: smen, aged salted butter (substitute: clarified butter plus a little salt is only an approximation)
warqa pastry for pastilla (substitute: phyllo dough, approximate)
Moroccan green or purple olives (substitute: good-quality brined green olives)
tips: Ras el hanout (usually variable mixture that may include cinnamon, ginger, turmeric, pepper, cardamom, nutmeg, mace, cloves, rose or other aromatics; there is no fixed formula): use about 5-10 g per 1 kg of stew ingredients when a recipe calls for a Moroccan mixed-spice profile; start low because blends vary. Salt: 0.0 g if the blend is explicitly salt-free; otherwise calculate from the package label. Do not assume all ras el hanout is salt-free.

Prepared chermoula (usually cilantro/coriander, parsley, garlic, cumin, paprika or chile, lemon and oil; formulas vary): about 60-100 g prepared chermoula can season 1 kg fish or vegetables in place of a freshly pounded marinade. Salt varies by brand: brand-dependent. Calculate salt-equivalent from the sodium label.

Harissa paste (usually red chile, garlic, spices and oil; it is Tunisian in origin but is used in parts of Morocco and the wider Maghreb): use roughly 10-20 g per 1 kg food when a Moroccan recipe specifically calls for harissa; do not use it as a universal Moroccan seasoning. Salt varies by brand: commercial pastes vary substantially; calculate from the label.
pitfalls: Do not treat Moroccan as synonymous with all North African or Maghrebi cooking.
Do not put harissa into every Moroccan dish; it is much more central to Tunisian cooking.
Do not treat ras el hanout as one standardized recipe or as a required seasoning for every tagine.
Do not make every Moroccan savory dish sweet with dried fruit and cinnamon.
Do not replace preserved lemon with an equal amount of fresh lemon and claim the result is equivalent.
Do not boil instant couscous and describe that method as the classic Moroccan couscous technique.
pantry: ground cumin, sweet paprika, ginger and turmeric
substitutes: salt-preserved lemon: no close substitute (fresh lemon gives acidity but not the fermented peel aroma or texture)

label: Tunisian
subtitle: Harissa, caraway, olive oil, couscous
about: On the Mediterranean coast between Algeria and Libya, Tunisia stretches from Cap Bon and Tunis to the inland steppes and Sahara. Amazigh, Arab, Andalusi, Ottoman and Mediterranean contacts shaped dishes that often feature olive oil, chili, grain dishes and seafood, with substantial regional variation. Representative dishes include fish couscous, lablabi, brik and kamounia.
flavors: tabil spice mixture or ground coriander (تابل, tābil)
hot red pepper (فلفل أحمر حار, filfil aḥmar ḥārr)
sweet_only: orange blossom water (ماء الزهر, māʾ al-zahr)
signature_ingredients: malsouka thin pastry sheets for brik (substitute: plain spring-roll wrappers; crispness and thickness differ)
ripe red Baklouti-type peppers for homemade harissa (substitute: red Fresno chilies, with red bell pepper to moderate heat; not an exact flavor match)
dried powdered jute mallow (mloukhiya) for its namesake stew (substitute: none; frozen molokhia or spinach produces a different texture and dish)
durum couscous for traditionally steamed couscous (substitute: plain supermarket couscous; adjust method because many boxes are presteamed)
tips: Ready-made harissa (red chili, garlic, coriander, caraway, salt): use 20 g prepared paste in place of 20 g homemade harissa as a starting point, then adjust heat and acidity; a typical packaged mix reporting 1.8 g salt per 100 g contributes about 0.36 g salt per 20 g, so check the label and subtract from separately added salt.

Pre-ground unsalted tabil or coriander-caraway blend (usually coriander and caraway, sometimes garlic and dried chili): replace 5 g freshly ground dry spice components with 5 g of a verified unsalted blend as a starting point (0 g salt); if salted, calculate salt from the package label.
pitfalls: Do not ban cumin from meat: kamounia may use it prominently.
Harissa is not merely a table sauce, but it also is not compulsory in every dish; recipes and heat levels vary.
Do not claim all Tunisian couscous is red or all Moroccan couscous pale.
Tabil may mean ground coriander alone or a variable coriander-based spice mix.
Do not equate hrous with a single standardized fermentation formula; regional fermentation details vary by maker.
Pantry defaults are soft assumptions; do not assume rarer specialty ingredients are on hand or that harissa must be used in every dish.

label: Algerian
subtitle: Dersa, frik, rechta, cinnamon
about: Algeria extends from Mediterranean cities such as Algiers, Oran and Constantine across the Atlas Mountains to the Sahara. Amazigh, Arab, Andalusi, Ottoman and later French influences shaped diverse regional traditions, including aromatic white sauces and chili-garlic red sauces. Representative dishes include rechta, chorba frik, chtitha djaj and couscous.
flavors: paprika or dried red pepper (فلفل عكري, felfel ʿakri)
ras el hanout mixed spices (راس الحانوت, rās el-ḥānūt)
sweet_only: orange blossom water (ماء الزهر, māʾ ez-zhar)
signature_ingredients: frik, roasted cracked green wheat, for chorba frik (substitute: coarse bulgur; texture is similar but lacks its green smoky aroma)
rechta, fine fresh semolina noodles prepared for steaming (substitute: fine fresh wheat noodles or tagliolini, preferably steamed rather than boiled if recipe permits)
dioul pastry sheets for bourek (substitute: spring-roll wrappers; expect a different texture)
berkoukes, large rolled semolina granules (substitute: large pearl couscous; size and hydration differ)
tips: Commercial unsalted ras el hanout (variable mixture of coriander, cumin, cinnamon, ginger, pepper and other spices): start with 5 g blend for 5 g of compatible dry mixed spices, not as a complete sauce substitute (0 g salt if unsalted; otherwise use labeled sodium).

Ready-made plain Tunisian harissa as an emergency dersa component (red chili, garlic, coriander, caraway and salt): use 15 g harissa plus about 5 g fresh garlic and 1 g ground cumin as a provisional stand-in for a chili-garlic dersa (not flavor-identical); a typical packaged mix at 1.8 g salt per 100 g contributes about 0.27 g salt per 15 g, so check the label and adjust added salt.
pitfalls: Avoid portraying one Algiers-style white sauce and one dersa-based red sauce as the entire country.
Moroccan cooks also have pale sauces and stuffed vegetable dishes; Ottoman history does not create an absolute culinary border.
Dersa has variants: do not insist paprika or cumin must be present in every mortar paste.
Rechta and frik are not interchangeable with ordinary boiled pasta and bulgur without changing results.
European mayonnaise-based Sauce Algérienne is not the same as traditional Algerian dersa.
Do not claim every recipe uses smen or a lemon-egg liaison.

label: Ethiopian
subtitle: Injera, berbere, wot, spiced butter
about: Ethiopia spans highlands around Addis Ababa and the northern plateau, the Rift Valley and hotter eastern and southern regions, so its food is highly regional. Highland Christian fasting practice, Muslim food traditions, indigenous crops and centuries of Red Sea and inland trade all contribute to a cuisine of fermented flatbreads, legumes, long-cooked onion stews, aromatic chile blends and spiced butter. Representative dishes include doro wot, misir wot, siga tibs and injera with vegetable and pulse dishes.
flavors: clarified butter infused with Ethiopian aromatics (ንጥር ቅቤ, niter qibe)
black cumin/nigella terminology varies by market (ጥቁር አዝሙድ, tikur azmud)
signature_ingredients: teff flour (substitute: none for traditional teff injera; buckwheat or millet can imitate some flavor but not the same fermentation, texture or identity)
shiro flour, roasted ground chickpea or pulse flour seasoned for shiro (substitute: plain chickpea flour plus separately added Ethiopian seasonings, approximate)
ayib, fresh Ethiopian curd cheese (substitute: well-drained farmer cheese or mild ricotta, approximate)
korerima, Ethiopian cardamom (substitute: none exact; ordinary green cardamom is distinctly different)
tips: Commercial berbere (usually dried chile with varying combinations of fenugreek, ginger, korerima/cardamom, coriander, cloves, cinnamon, garlic and other spices): use about 10-25 g per 1 kg finished stew ingredients depending on heat and concentration; classic wot can use more, so taste and recipe context matter. Salt: 0.0 g only for a product labeled salt-free. Some blends contain salt, so calculate from the label.

Commercial niter qibe (usually clarified butter infused with combinations of korerima, koseret, besobela, fenugreek, ginger, garlic and other aromatics): replace plain cooking butter or fat 1:1 by weight when the recipe calls for niter qibe; 20 g commercial niter qibe replaces 20 g homemade. Salt: usually little or no added salt in traditional formulations, but packaged products vary; verify label.

Commercial mekelesha (usually warm finishing spices such as korerima/cardamom, cinnamon, cloves, black pepper, cumin, long pepper or nutmeg): use about 1-3 g per 1 kg stew near the end of cooking rather than substituting it for berbere. Salt: usually 0.0 g if sold as a pure spice blend; verify label.
pitfalls: Do not put berbere into every Ethiopian dish; alicha and many vegetable or fasting dishes follow different seasoning patterns.
Do not put butter into Orthodox Christian fasting dishes.
Do not treat ordinary green cardamom as an exact replacement for korerima.
Do not call an unfermented pancake or wheat tortilla injera.
Do not make wot like a quick curry; extended onion cooking is a defining structural technique.
Do not collapse Ethiopian and Eritrean cuisines into one undifferentiated recipe tradition even though they share many foods.

label: Egyptian
subtitle: Ful, ta'ameya, molokhia, cumin, garlic
about: Egyptian cooking follows the Nile Valley and Delta from Upper Egypt to Cairo, Alexandria and the Mediterranean coast, with additional traditions in oases and desert communities. Ancient agricultural continuity, Coptic and Islamic traditions, Ottoman rule and Mediterranean migration all contributed to a cuisine especially rich in breads, legumes, vegetables, garlic, cumin and coriander. Representative dishes include ful medames, fava-bean ta'ameya, molokhia and koshari.
flavors: coriander seed and fresh coriander (كزبرة, kozbara)
pounded spice-and-seed mixture with highly variable formulas (دقة, duqqa)
signature_ingredients: molokhia leaves, Corchorus/Jute mallow (substitute: none exact; spinach does not reproduce the characteristic mucilaginous texture)
small dried fava beans for ful (substitute: canned fava beans, with loss of some texture from long simmering)
split dried fava beans for ta'ameya (substitute: none if the dish is to remain classically Egyptian ta'ameya; chickpeas produce a different falafel tradition)
baladi bread (substitute: whole-wheat pita, approximate)
tips: Prepared dukkah/dokka (usually variable toasted coriander, cumin, sesame and pepper; many versions add nigella, nuts, sumac or other seeds): use 5-15 g as a finishing seasoning rather than as a universal Egyptian spice blend. Salt: uncertain across brands for generic dukkah because formulas vary. Pure unsalted mixes contribute 0.0 g; packaged salted versions require label calculation.

Prepared tahini (usually ground sesame seed, sometimes only sesame and sometimes added salt): replace homemade sesame paste 1:1 by weight; 30 g prepared tahini replaces 30 g homemade. Salt: 0.0 g only if the ingredient list is sesame alone; otherwise calculate from label.

Canned ful/fava beans (usually cooked fava beans, water and often salt): about 240 g drained canned fava beans can replace roughly 80-100 g dry beans after cooking, but texture and flavor differ. Salt varies by brand: highly brand-dependent; rinse and calculate from label rather than assuming a fixed value.
pitfalls: Do not use chickpeas as the default base for Egyptian ta'ameya; fava beans are the classic Egyptian distinction.
Do not treat dukkah as a single standardized recipe.
Do not replace molokhia with spinach and call the texture equivalent.
Do not force a generic Levantine hummus-tabbouleh flavor template onto Egyptian dishes.
Do not turn koshari into one-pot spiced rice; its separately prepared components and sauces are central to the dish.
Do not assume Egyptian savory food is heavily perfumed with cinnamon, cardamom and allspice; garlic, cumin, coriander, onion, chile, lemon and vinegar are often more characteristic.

label: Nigerian
subtitle: Peppers, fermented beans, soups, smoke
about: Nigeria stretches from the Atlantic mangrove and Niger Delta coast through humid forest zones to the savanna and Sahel, with Lagos, the Yoruba southwest, Igbo southeast and Hausa-speaking north representing only part of its culinary diversity. Hundreds of ethnic communities, long-distance West African trade, Atlantic exchange and British colonial history created many distinct soup, stew, grain, tuber, bean and grilled-food traditions rather than one uniform national pantry. Representative dishes include jollof rice, egusi soup, pepper soup and suya.
flavors: category of pungent fermented seed condiments (ogiri)
dry spice mixture associated especially with suya (yaji)
signature_ingredients: egusi, oil-rich melon seeds (substitute: hulled pepitas can approximate body and nuttiness but are not equivalent)
ogbono, Irvingia kernels (substitute: none; its characteristic draw/slippery thickening behavior is distinctive)
garri, roasted fermented cassava granules (substitute: none)
white African yam, Dioscorea rotundata (substitute: none exact; US orange sweet potato is not the same ingredient)
ugu, fluted pumpkin leaves (substitute: spinach or kale, approximate and dish-dependent)
unrefined red palm oil (substitute: none exact; neutral oil lacks its flavor and color)
tips: Commercial yaji or suya spice (usually chile, ginger and aromatic spices; yajin kuli or many suya blends also contain ground kulikuli/peanut): use about 20-40 g blend per 1 kg sliced meat, depending on concentration. Salt varies by brand: commercial blends vary and many are salted. Calculate from label; do not assume zero. Treat peanut status as mandatory label data.

Pepper-soup spice blend (usually variable combinations of uda, ehuru, uziza, alligator pepper and other regional spices): use about 5-12 g per liter of soup as a starting range, then adjust to the blend. Salt: 0.0 g for a clearly labeled pure spice blend; many commercial products add salt, so verify.

Bouillon cube or seasoning powder (usually salt, flavor enhancers, spices and flavorings; some contain soy, wheat or milk-derived ingredients): do not replace herbs or indigenous fermented seasonings 1:1 with bouillon. When a recipe explicitly uses it, dose according to the label and reduce separate salt. Salt: no reliable generic value. Calculate salt-equivalent from the product's sodium label; brand differences are too large for a safe fixed number.
pitfalls: Do not model Nigeria as one uniform cuisine; regional and ethnic distinctions are fundamental.
Do not add egusi, crayfish, palm oil or iru to every Nigerian soup or stew.
Do not assume all yaji formulations are identical, and do not miss the common peanut component in suya seasoning.
Do not substitute orange sweet potato for Nigerian white yam and call it yam without qualification.
Do not use generic Indian curry powder as the defining flavor of Nigerian cooking even though Nigerian-style curry powder and dried thyme are common in some modern dishes.
Do not describe jollof rice as the sole or universal centerpiece of Nigerian food.
pantry: red palm oil and neutral oil

label: Senegalese
subtitle: Rice, fish, onion, peanut, fermentation
about: Senegal faces the Atlantic at Africa's westernmost bulge, with Dakar on the Cap-Vert peninsula, Saint-Louis near the Senegal River and Casamance south of The Gambia. Wolof, Lebou, Serer, Fulani, Mandinka, Jola and other communities, Atlantic trade, Islam and French colonial commerce all shaped a cuisine famous for deeply seasoned rice, fish, onion sauces, peanuts and fermented condiments. Representative dishes include ceebu jën, yassa, mafé and soupou kandia.
flavors: dried or fermented fish used as a savory seasoning (guedj)
pounded parsley-garlic-chile herb mixture used especially to season or stuff fish (rof)
pounded aromatic seasoning base, formulas varying by cook (nokoss)
signature_ingredients: broken rice used for ceebu jën (substitute: ordinary long-grain rice is usable but gives a different absorption and texture)
jaxatu/diakhatou, small bitter African eggplant (substitute: none exact; small eggplant plus a bitter green is only an approximation)
fonio (substitute: quinoa or fine couscous can fill a structural role but are not flavor-equivalent)
cassava root (substitute: none exact; potato changes both texture and flavor)
natural unsweetened peanut paste (substitute: unsweetened smooth peanut butter)
tips: Prepared nokoss (usually garlic, onion or scallion, chile, pepper and parsley, sometimes ginger, nététou, bay or other aromatics): use about 40-80 g prepared nokoss per 1 kg main ingredients as a starting point, depending on concentration. Salt varies by brand: homemade nokoss may be unsalted or salted, while commercial products vary. Calculate from label.

Commercial bouillon cube or seasoning powder (usually salt, flavor enhancers, spices and flavorings; ingredient profiles vary widely): use only when the intended Senegalese recipe calls for bouillon; do not treat it as a replacement for nététou, guedj or yët. Salt: no safe generic value. Calculate salt-equivalent from sodium on the label and reduce separate salt accordingly.

Prepared peanut butter for mafé (usually ground peanuts; US products may additionally contain sugar, salt and stabilizers): use natural unsweetened peanut butter 1:1 by weight for Senegalese peanut paste; 100 g peanut butter replaces 100 g peanut paste. Salt: 0.0 g if made from peanuts only; otherwise use the nutrition label.
pitfalls: Do not turn every Senegalese dish into a peanut stew; mafé is one important family, not the whole cuisine.
Do not treat yassa as simply lemon chicken; the large quantity of onions, marination and often grilling are defining.
Do not replace the fermented savory ingredients in ceebu jën automatically with soy sauce or Southeast Asian fish sauce.
Do not treat rof and nokoss as identical even though their ingredients overlap.
Do not hard-code the story that Penda Mbaye definitively invented ceebu jën; Saint-Louis origin is well established, while single-inventor attribution is better treated as tradition.
Do not assume ceebu jën, yassa, mafé and dibi all use the same seasoning profile.

label: South African
subtitle: Pap, braai, Cape Malay, Durban curry
about: Stretching from the Atlantic and Indian Ocean coasts around Cape Town and Durban across the Drakensberg escarpment to the Highveld around Johannesburg and the Orange and Limpopo river basins, South Africa encompasses distinct coastal, mountain, and interior foodways. Indigenous Xhosa, Zulu, and Sotho-Tswana grain-and-greens cooking met 17th-century Dutch settlement, enslaved and exiled Southeast Asian and Indian cooks at the Cape, and 19th-century Indian indentured laborers in KwaZulu-Natal, producing a multi-tradition cuisine spanning wood-fired grilled meats, slow-simmered maize and bean dishes, sweet-sour Cape stews, and fiery coastal curries. Representative dishes include umngqusho (samp and sugar beans), Cape Malay bobotie, potjiekos and braai boerewors, and Durban curry served in a hollowed-out bunny chow loaf.
flavors: Cape Malay and Durban curry masalas (kerriepoeier / masala)
cloves, nutmeg, and allspice (naeltjies, neutmuskaat, piment)
bird's eye chile and peri-peri sauce (piri-piri)
garlic and fresh ginger (knoffel en gemmer)
sweet_only: naartjie peel (naartjieskil, mainly in melktert, koesisters, and preserves, though historically used in some savory Cape stews)
signature_ingredients: white maize meal, coarse or fine (mieliemeel / impuphu) (substitute: white cornmeal or coarse white grits, with minor texture differences)
samp, coarsely cracked de-hulled dried corn kernels (substitute: dried white hominy or posole kernels, soaked and simmered longer)
speckled sugar beans (substitute: dried cranberry beans or pinto beans)
amasi or maas, thick cultured soured whole milk (substitute: plain whole-milk kefir or cultured buttermilk)
morogo or imifino, wild or cultivated leafy greens such as amaranth and pumpkin leaves (substitute: swiss chard, collard greens, or mature spinach)

boerewors, fresh coiled coriander-and-vinegar beef-and-pork sausage (substitute: none exact; coarsely ground beef and pork sausage seasoned with toasted coriander, cloves, nutmeg, and vinegar approximates it)
biltong, air-dried vinegar-and-coriander-cured beef strips (substitute: none; commercial beef jerky is usually sweeter and smoked rather than air-dried with coriander and vinegar)
waterblommetjies, aquatic Cape pondweed buds used in traditional bredie (substitute: none exact; trimmed green beans or young artichoke hearts approximate the vegetable role)
tips: Packaged South African curry powder or Durban masala: usually contains ground coriander, turmeric, cumin, chiles, fenugreek, paprika, cinnamon or cassia, ginger, cloves, and sometimes wheat flour or bran as a carrier. Swap 15 to 25 g dry blend per 1 kg meat or vegetables in curries or bobotie, or 50 to 80 g wet curry paste per 1 kg ingredients. Pure dry curry powders usually supply under 0.1 g salt per 100 g, whereas wet curry pastes vary substantially by brand (uncertain across brands for paste sodium; check the label and figure about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium).

Commercial braai spice or seasoned braai salt: usually contains coarse sea or table salt, toasted coriander, paprika, black pepper, dried onion and garlic, sugar or dextrose, MSG or yeast extract, and sometimes mustard powder or vegetable oil. Rub 10 to 15 g per 1 kg meat or vegetables in place of separate salt and dry spices. Salt content ranges widely from roughly 50 g to 95 g salt per 100 g depending on whether sold as a spice rub or seasoned braai salt (uncertain across brands across brands; read the nutrition panel using about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium and withhold extra salt until tasting).

Commercial boerewors sausage seasoning mix: usually contains salt, coarsely ground roasted coriander, black pepper, nutmeg, cloves, allspice, sugar or dextrose, wheat rusk or cereal binder, MSG, and often sulfite preservatives. Mix about 20 to 30 g dry seasoning with 40 to 50 ml vinegar per 1 kg coarse ground beef and pork instead of separate coriander, warm spices, and salt. Typical commercial packs run roughly 40 to 43 g salt per 100 g, around 15,000 to 17,000 mg sodium per 100 g (uncertain across brands across butcher and retail blends; verify the label at about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium and omit additional salt).

Packaged brown onion soup powder (commonly used to thicken potjiekos and stews): usually contains cornstarch or wheat flour, salt, dehydrated onion, sugar, MSG or yeast extract, caramel color, and hydrolyzed vegetable or soy protein. Whisk 45 to 50 g dry powder into 250 ml water per 1.5 kg stew to thicken and season in place of flour and browned-onion stock. Standard US dry onion soup mixes average around 20 g salt per 100 g (roughly 8,000 mg sodium per 100 g), though South African packets subject to mandatory national sodium limits may contain less (uncertain across brands across US vs South African formulations; calculate from the label at about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium and hold extra salt until tasting).

Store-bought fruit chutney or mango atchar: fruit chutney usually contains dried peaches or apricots, sugar, vinegar, onion, and warm spices, while mango atchar usually contains green mango, vegetable oil, mustard seed, fenugreek, turmeric, garlic, and chiles. Use 30 to 60 g fruit chutney in bobotie or glazes, or 15 to 30 g atchar as a sharp side condiment or stirred into beans and curries. Commercial fruit chutneys commonly supply roughly 1 g to 1.8 g salt per 100 g (though reduced-sodium versions can be under 0.2 g), while oil-cured mango atchars are far saltier at roughly 8 g to 12.5 g salt per 100 g (uncertain across brands across brands; check the label using about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium).
pitfalls: Do not treat Cape Malay and Durban curries as interchangeable; Cape Malay dishes usually emphasize warm sweet spices and fruit or vinegar balance, whereas Durban curries are fiery red, oil-topped, and dairy-free.
Do not thicken traditional Durban curries with coconut milk or heavy cream in the style of Thai or North Indian restaurant dishes.
Do not collapse crumbly phuthu, smooth stiff pap, and fermented sorghum ting into a single uniform maize porridge.
Do not assume South African home cooking is all grilled meat; Indigenous staples such as umngqusho and morogo and vegetarian bean curries are everyday foundations.
Do not put pork into Cape Malay or Muslim Durban dishes, or beef into Hindu-tradition Durban curries, even though both meats are common in Afrikaans and many Indigenous kitchens.
pantry: ground coriander, turmeric, cumin, and curry powder
fruit chutney and smooth apricot jam
cider or spirit vinegar and Worcestershire sauce

label: East African
subtitle: Ugali, nyama choma, tamarind, coconut pilau
about: Kenya and Tanzania span the Indian Ocean coast—including Mombasa, Lamu, Dar es Salaam and the Zanzibar archipelago—and rise inland past Mount Kilimanjaro and Mount Kenya to the Great Rift Valley, Nairobi and Lake Victoria. Bantu, Nilotic and Cushitic farming and pastoralist communities, centuries of Indian Ocean dhow trade with Omani Arab, Persian and South Asian merchants, and Columbian Exchange crops shaped distinct coastal and highland cooking traditions. Inland kitchens often pair mild maize staples, braised leafy greens, legumes and charcoal-roasted meat with fresh relishes, while Swahili coastal dishes frequently layer fresh coconut milk, tamarind and warm whole spices; representative dishes include ugali with sukuma wiki, nyama choma, githeri and Swahili coconut-cardamom pilau.
flavors: hot bird's-eye or Scotch-bonnet-type chile (pilipili kichaa / pilipili mbuzi)
signature_ingredients: fine white maize meal for ugali, sifted sembe or whole-grain dona (substitute: finely ground white cornmeal; yellow cornmeal changes flavor and color, and coarse polenta gives a different texture)
freshly pressed coconut milk, tui la nazi (substitute: canned unsweetened full-fat coconut milk, using the thick top cream for tui la kwanza and thinned milk for tui la pili)
dried or fresh pigeon peas, mbaazi (substitute: dried or canned pigeon peas from international aisles, or black-eyed peas for a similar legume stew)
green cooking bananas or unripe plantains, ndizi mbichi (substitute: firm green plantains)
pounded cassava leaves, kisamvu (substitute: none exact; collard greens or spinach do not match the texture or flavor)
sun-dried small freshwater fish, omena or dagaa (substitute: none exact; dried anchovies or dried smelts fill a related savory dried-fish role with different size and flavor)
unripe green papaya for tenderizing mishkaki (substitute: plain grated kiwi or fresh pineapple applied very briefly, though flavor differs)
tips: Commercial mchuzi seasoning and thickener mix (usually contains cornstarch, iodized salt, sugar, MSG and flavor enhancers, dried garlic, ginger, coriander, cumin, turmeric, cinnamon and meat flavoring or coloring): dissolve about 10-20 g in cold water per 1 kg stew ingredients as a quick savory gravy thickener for everyday inland stews, rather than as a substitute for whole coastal spices. Salt: varies widely because commercial mixes vary across markets and formulations (some retail packets report roughly 11-12 g salt or around 4,500 mg sodium per 100 g, roughly 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium), so check the package label and reduce separately added salt.

Packaged pilau masala spice blend (usually contains ground cumin, cardamom, cinnamon or cassia, cloves and black pepper, sometimes with coriander, nutmeg or bay leaf): use about 10-20 g per 1 kg rice and meat in place of freshly toasted and ground whole pilau spices. Salt: 0.0 g only when labeled pure spice; uncertain across brands for mixed retail packets that may include salt or fillers, so verify the nutrition label.

Commercial bouillon cubes or seasoning powder (usually contains salt, vegetable fat, starch, MSG or yeast extract, onion, spices and meat or vegetable flavorings): use only when a recipe explicitly calls for stock or bouillon (about 4-5 g per 500 ml liquid), and do not use it to replace coconut milk, tamarind or aromatic pilau spices. Salt: varies widely because sodium varies widely by brand (standard 4.5-5 g cubes often contain roughly 900-1,150 mg sodium, or about 2.2-2.9 g salt per cube at roughly 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium), so calculate from the package label and adjust separate salt.

Prepared tamarind paste or concentrate (usually concentrated tamarind pulp and water, sometimes with salt or preservatives): use about 15-30 g thinned in warm water per 1 kg fish, stew or sauce in place of soaking and straining raw tamarind pods, adjusting to taste because acidity varies. Salt: usually near 0.0 g for pure unsalted tamarind paste (roughly 24-28 mg sodium, well under 0.1 g salt, per 100 g), though uncertain across brands for seasoned commercial jars that add salt; check the label.
pitfalls: Do not confuse Kenyan and Tanzanian cooking with Ethiopian or Eritrean cuisines by adding berbere, niter qibe or injera.
Do not treat Swahili coastal coconut-and-spice cooking as identical to inland highland cooking built around ugali, sukuma wiki, githeri and nyama choma.

Do not merge Swahili pilau and Swahili biryani into the same method: pilau is usually a deeply browned one-pot rice dish, whereas biryani layers separately cooked spiced meat curry with parboiled rice.
Do not make every Kenyan or Tanzanian dish heavily chili-hot; everyday ugali, sukuma wiki and coconut bean dishes are often mild, with heat served on the side as pilipili or kachumbari.
Do not automatically add generic curry powder or coconut milk to inland classics like nyama choma, ugali or traditional githeri.
pantry: cardamom, cloves, cinnamon, cumin and turmeric

label: Ghanaian
subtitle: Banku, shito, groundnut, smoked fish
about: Ghana stretches from the Gulf of Guinea coast around Accra and the Volta River basin through humid forest zones around Kumasi to the drier northern savanna around Tamale. Akan, Ga-Dangme, Ewe, Mole-Dagbani, and other communities, alongside trans-Saharan commerce and the Atlantic exchange that brought maize, cassava, tomatoes, chiles, and peanuts, shaped a cooking tradition built on fermented or pounded starchy staples paired with richly layered soups, tomato stews, and pungent condiments. Representative dishes include banku with grilled tilapia and pepper sauces, fufu with groundnut or palm nut soup, waakye, and Ghanaian jollof rice.
flavors: grains of paradise or alligator pepper (fom wisa)
Scotch bonnet or local aromatic green chile (kpakpo shito / mako)
signature_ingredients: fermented corn dough and cassava dough for banku and kenkey (substitute: none exact; unfermented cornmeal or masa harina lacks the lactic tang and cohesive stretch)
fresh oil palm fruit pulp and unrefined red palm oil for abenkwan and stews (substitute: canned palm fruit concentrate for soup; neutral oil lacks red palm oil flavor and color)
dried sorghum leaves (waakye leaves) for waakye (substitute: none exact; a pinch of baking soda mimics the alkaline effect on black-eyed peas without the burgundy color or earthy aroma)
cocoyam leaves (kontomire) for kontomire stew and ebunuebunu soup (substitute: fresh spinach or collard greens, approximate)
african garden eggs, small bitter-sweet eggplants (substitute: Thai or small globe eggplants, approximate)
white African yam (Dioscorea rotundata) and green plantain for fufu and ampesi (substitute: none exact for white yam, as orange sweet potato is distinct; green plantains are common in Latin markets)
agushie, ground oil-rich melon seeds for palava sauce (substitute: hulled pepitas approximate body but are not flavor-equivalent)
tips: Jarred shito (usually vegetable oil, onions, dried chiles, ginger, garlic, tomato paste, dried shrimp, dried smoked fish or herring, spices, and salt or bouillon): use 15 to 30 g as a condiment per serving or 20 to 40 g to season a pan of rice or stew base in place of homemade shito. Salt estimate is varies widely because commercial jars vary widely (often roughly 800 to 2,300 mg sodium per 100 g, or roughly 2.0 to 5.8 g salt per 100 g, computed at about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium); check the nutrition label and reduce added salt.

Canned palm fruit concentrate or palm nut soup base (usually pressed oil palm fruit pulp, water, and often added salt): dilute roughly 400 g canned concentrate with 700 to 1,000 ml stock and water to replace boiling and pounding fresh palm nuts for abenkwan. Salt estimate is varies widely because some cans are unsalted while salted imports often report around 150 to 180 mg sodium per 100 to 133 g serving (about 0.38 to 0.45 g salt per serving at about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium); taste before salting, especially when cooking with koobi or momoni.

Instant fufu flour or dehydrated plantain-cassava or yam flour (usually dehydrated cassava, plantain, or yam starch, sometimes with stabilizers): whisk 100 g dry flour into roughly 350 to 450 ml hot water and stir over medium-low heat to approximate pounded fufu without a mortar, though stretch and aroma differ. Salt is usually 0.0 g for pure dehydrated root and plantain flours, though seasoned blends vary; verify the ingredient list.

Commercial bouillon cube or shrimp seasoning powder (usually salt, flavor enhancers, vegetable or palm fat, starch, spices, and sometimes soy, wheat, or milk derivatives): use only when a modern recipe calls for commercial seasoning rather than replacing dawadawa or momoni 1:1; dose by package directions and reduce or omit separate salt. Salt estimate is varies widely because brand formulations vary substantially (check the sodium line and use about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium).
pitfalls: Do not treat Ghanaian and Nigerian jollof as identical; Ghanaian cooks usually use fragrant jasmine or basmati rice rather than parboiled long-grain rice and rarely aim for a charred firewood flavor.
Do not assume Ghanaian cooking is uniformly peanut-based or palm-oil-based; light soup (nkrakra), tomato stews, and northern millet-based tuo zaafi follow distinct fat and seasoning patterns.
Do not substitute Southeast Asian fish sauce or oyster sauce for Ghanaian momoni, koobi, or dried shrimp without noting the major difference in cured aroma and saltiness.
Do not replace white African yam (Dioscorea rotundata) with orange sweet potato without clarifying that they differ substantially in texture and sweetness.
Do not omit the lactic sourness of fermented maize and cassava dough when writing banku or kenkey recipes by presenting unfermented cornmeal or grits as equivalent.
pantry: red palm oil and neutral oil

label: Central African
subtitle: Palm butter, cassava leaves, njangsang
about: Stretching from Cameroon's volcanic highlands and Atlantic coast across Gabon's equatorial rainforests to the vast Congo River basin and cities such as Douala, Libreville, Brazzaville, and Kinshasa, Central African cooking is anchored in forest, river, and coastal ecologies. Bantu-speaking and forest-dwelling communities built traditions around palm oil, wild forest seeds, river fish, and plantains, later reshaped by Portuguese and transatlantic introductions of cassava, peanuts, and chiles alongside French and Belgian urban influences into slow-simmered stews, pounded greens, and leaf-wrapped steamed dishes. Representative dishes include pondu (or saka-saka), poulet moambe (or nyembwe), Cameroonian ndolé, and fish liboké served with fufu or chikwangue.
flavors: hot bird's-eye or habanero chile (pili-pili / pilipili)
penja white or black pepper (poivre de Penja)
commercial bouillon cubes or powder (cube d'assaisonnement)
sweet_only: used mainly in mikate beignets, sweet porridges, and drinks (vanilla)
signature_ingredients: palm nut pulp / moambe cream (substitute: unsweetened natural peanut butter blended with unrefined red palm oil and sweet paprika, which shifts the flavor toward groundnut stew)
unrefined red palm oil (substitute: none exact; neutral oil tinted with annatto mimics color only without the earthy berry-like flavor)
cassava leaves for pondu or saka-saka (substitute: finely chopped collard greens, kale, or turnip greens mixed with spinach; lacks cassava leaves' nutty bitterness and requires a shorter simmer)
bitterleaf / Vernonia amygdalina for ndolé (substitute: none exact; well-washed dandelion greens or mustard greens mixed with spinach approximate some bitterness)
chikwangue / bobolo fermented cassava loaves (substitute: none; plain boiled cassava or steamed rice serves as a different starchy accompaniment)
odika / wild mango seed paste (substitute: ground ogbono / Irvingia gabonensis if available, otherwise none)
fumbua / okok / Gnetum africanum shredded wild leaves (substitute: finely shredded kale or collard greens, which lack the chewy texture)
smoked river fish or dried stockfish / salted cod (makayabu) (substitute: smoked mackerel or dried salted cod/bacalao soaked to desalinate)
marantaceae or banana leaves for liboké wrapping (substitute: parchment paper sealed inside aluminum foil for steaming)
tips: Commercial canned palm nut cream or palm soup base (moambe or nyembwe paste): plain cans usually contain extracted oil palm fruit pulp and water (occasionally with added salt), while prepared soup bases may include salt, spices, or bouillon. Swap by weight: use 200-400 g canned palm cream per 1 kg poultry or meat, thinning with water or stock to stew consistency. Salt: varies widely because plain cans may have near-zero salt while seasoned palm soup bases vary widely by brand; check the label and calculate about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium before adding extra salt or bouillon.

Commercial bouillon cubes or powder: usually contain salt (commonly 40% to 76% by weight in regional nutrition analyses), monosodium glutamate, hydrolyzed vegetable protein or yeast extract, palm fat, starch, and dried aromatics. Swap by weight: use roughly 4-10 g (about half to one standard cube depending on cube size) per 1 kg stew or soup in place of salt and stock base. Salt: uncertain across brands across brands, as regional cubes often supply about 900 to over 1,000 mg sodium per cube (roughly 2.2 to 2.5 g salt, calculated at about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium); verify the package label and omit or sharply reduce separately added salt.

Frozen pre-pounded cassava leaves: usually contain shredded or pounded cassava leaves (almost always pre-blanched before freezing, though package instructions vary) and water, without added spices. Swap by weight: replace fresh pounded cassava leaves 1:1 by weight (typically 450-900 g frozen leaves for a family pot), thawing and simmering 45 to 90 minutes to ensure tenderness and full breakdown. Salt: usually 0 g in plain frozen packs; verify the label for seasoned packs and calculate about 2.5 g salt per 1,000 mg sodium if seasoned.
pitfalls: Do not treat canned palm nut cream (moambe/nyembwe) and clear unrefined red palm oil as interchangeable; palm cream provides thick body and emulsion while red palm oil is a cooking fat.

Do not confuse Central African country onion (Afrostyrax lepidophyllus, rondelle) with calabash nutmeg (Monodora myristica, pèbè); they are distinct spices with garlic-truffle versus nutmeg-like aromas.

Do not substitute raw, quickly sautéed spinach for cassava leaves or bitterleaf without adjusting technique; traditional pondu and ndolé require extended simmering or multi-stage washing to remove bitterness and cyanogenic compounds.

Do not assume Central African cuisine is uniform across Cameroon, Gabon, and the Congos or identical to West African cooking; signature ingredients such as odika, mbongo, and Penja pepper are strongly localized.
Do not omit soaking and rinsing salted fish (makayabu) or add full table salt alongside commercial bouillon cubes and ground crayfish, which easily over-salts stews.
